opening.headline: We explain why AI plausibly cites non-existent papers using the principle of how models create answers, and learn how to reduce errors.
body: It is not uncommon to hear that the AI answer had the paper title, author, and page number written down in detail, so I transferred it to the report as is, but when I searched, the paper did not exist. The more confident your answer is, the more difficult it is to be suspicious.

In this class, we will first look at the principle that the model does not retrieve facts, but selects the next token based on probability and continues sentences. We then break down whether hallucination comes from a knowledge base, lack of context, or creation method, and even outline how to say you don't know and how to check the source.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the principle that the model selects the next token with probability
It is possible to distinguish whether hallucination comes from a knowledge cutoff, lack of context, or generation method.

screens.title: A plausible but non-existent thesis
screens.lead: Read the AI answer below. Select an underlined passage and an explanation will appear explaining why you should check it.

visual.alt: A scene where the paper title, author, and page number are underlined with a highlighter in the AI answer card.

data.text: Regarding the productivity effects of remote work, the Research team including Seojin Han announced in 2023 paper 「Changes in work engagement in a distributed work environment」 (Korean Organizational Research Volume 18, Number 2, pages 41-67) is representative. This study reported that engagement increased after the introduction of remote work.

marks.span: 「Changes in work engagement in a distributed work environment」
marks.note: This is the title of the paper. If you actually search, the paper with this title may not exist. The title is easy to create by stringing together plausible words.

marks.span: Research team including Seojin Han announced in 2023
marks.note: Author and year can also be constructed in the same way. The fact that it has a specific name and year written on it is not proof of its existence.

The volume number and page number look more reliable because the format is elaborate, but it may be the result of probabilistic succession. Information cannot be confirmed until it is directly compared to the original text and link.

screens.outro: Let us first approach why this phenomenon occurs by considering the difference between AI and search engines.

screens.title: Think about the difference between search engines and AI answers.
screens.lead: Read the questions below slowly and answer them in your head. There are no fields to enter or submit.

visual.alt: A scene where the image of the search window on the left and the image of the chat window on the right are placed side by side.

paragraphs: How would you describe the difference between search engines and AI answers in one sentence?

Search engines find documents that already exist and display them in a list. So where does AI get its answers? Does it retrieve the correct answer stored somewhere, or is it created in some other way?

There is no right answer. However, it would be good to compare how your initial thoughts on this question change on subsequent screens. On this screen, don't write down your answer, just think about it.

callout.label: Organizing the instructor's thoughts
callout.text: The search engine finds existing documents, and generative AI creates new sentences based on learned patterns. If you understand this difference, you will be able to see that the case in the previous paper is not a random mistake, but a phenomenon resulting from the method.

screens.outro: Now, let's take a step-by-step look at the process by which the model creates sentences.

screens.title: Select the next token with probability
screens.lead: When you select a number marker in the picture, a description of each part of the model's sentence-writing process will appear. Please check them one by one starting from number 1.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the beginning of a sentence, next token candidates and probability bars, and how the selected token appears at the end of the sentence.
labels: Probability figures are examples for explanation.

markers.label: Sentences so far
markers.title: Read the first part of the sentence
markers.body: The model reads the input sentences and the sentences created so far. This is the context that serves as the basis for determining the next token. If there is no data to confirm the facts in this context, the model will continue to rely only on the learned patterns.

markers.label: Candidates and Probability
markers.title: Calculate the likelihood for each candidate token
markers.body: The model sets possible tokens as candidates and calculates the probability of how likely each candidate is. The figures in the picture are examples for illustrative purposes. The point is that the most likely candidate is not always the truth.

markers.label: choose one
markers.title: choose one of them
markers.body: Candidates with higher odds are chosen more often, but the same candidates are not always chosen. So, if you send the same question multiple times, the token you choose may change and the sentence expression may change.

markers.label: Add to the end of a sentence
markers.title: Attach the selected token and repeat again.
markers.body: Once the selected token is attached to the end of the sentence, the model rereads the extended sentence and selects the next token in the same way. OpenAI help explains that the model creates useful responses based on patterns in the data it has learned. In other words, sentences are not the result of taking out facts, but the result of stringing them together in a plausible way.

screens.outro: Let's compare what it looks like in practice if we ask the same question multiple times.

screens.title: Same question three times: different sentences, mixed numbers
screens.lead: This is an example response obtained by asking the same question three times. Select each tab, read it, and compare what parts are similar and different.

tabs.label: Reply 1
tabs.body:
Question: How does working from home affect my productivity?

Answer 1: Working from home often has a positive impact on productivity, with less travel time and more time to focus. However, in tasks that require collaboration, communication costs can increase, so the effectiveness varies depending on the nature of the task.

The key conclusion is that it depends on the nature of the job.

tabs.label: Reply 2
tabs.body:
Answer 2: The effectiveness of working from home depends on the type of work. This is a great advantage for tasks that you can focus on alone, but it can actually cause delays in tasks that require immediate exchange of opinions.

The sentence expression is different from answer 1, but the conclusion is the same. This is a natural result of the method of selecting tokens based on probability that the core is maintained and only the expression is changed.

tabs.label: Reply 3
tabs.body:
Answer 3: Companies that introduced telecommuting saw an average increase in productivity of 23%, with the effect being particularly significant in development positions. However, the effect may vary in collaboration-oriented work.

This response alone contains the specific number 'average 23%'. No source is given and other responses do not have the same figures.

tabs.label: Comparison results
tabs.body:
The conclusions of the three responses are the same, but the wording is different. It is normal for the expressions to differ. However, the numbers may vary from response to response or may only appear in one response, in which case you should be suspicious of possible baselessness.

Claude's documentation explains that if you run the same prompt, or request to the model, multiple times and compare the results, you can spot hallucinations as discrepancies. The starting point for confirmation is to divide the consistent and unstable parts.

screens.outro: So where do these errors come from? Let’s break it down into three roots.

screens.title: The three roots of hallucination
screens.lead: The following flashcards explain three causes of hallucination. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

visual.alt: Three card icons representing a calendar, blank document, and dice respectively.

cards.back: This is a phenomenon in which a model creates plausible information that is different from the facts or does not exist. OpenAI Help cites examples of incorrect definitions or dates, made-up citations and non-existent references, and overconfident answers to vague or complex questions.

The model is trained only on data up to the point at which it was trained. You won't know what happened after that unless you use a search tool. If you are asked something you don't know, you can answer with old information or fill in the gaps with similar information.

If the input does not contain the data required for an answer, the model fills in the blanks with a guess. The more you ask for specific facts without providing supporting documents, the more dangerous it is. Conversely, providing the necessary documentation also reduces this risk.

The model selects the next token with probability and continues the sentence. So, speaking confidently does not mean being accurate. The OpenAI help also explains that the model can express high confidence even in wrong answers.

screens.outro: Let’s break down the cause by applying these three to one actual answer.

screens.title: Explanation: Breaking down answers mixed with made-up sources by cause
screens.lead: The instructor checks the initial paper citation answers one by one according to three roots. Move to the next step with the right arrow.

steps.title: Check case
steps.body: The answer to be analyzed is a sentence presented based on “Changes in Work Engagement in a Distributed Work Environment” published in 2023 by Seojin Han and other researchers (Korean Organization Studies Vol. 18, No. 2, pp. 41-67). The questioner did not provide thesis materials. These answers are checked in the following order: knowledge cutoff, context, and creation method.

steps.title: Step 1: Check the knowledge cutoff
steps.body: We check whether the paper is the latest research published after the time the model was trained. In this case, the year 2023 is written, but it is closer to creating a paper that does not exist in the first place rather than saying it is wrong because they do not know the latest paper. Therefore, the reference date is viewed as a secondary factor rather than the main cause.

steps.title: Step 2: Check context
steps.body: The key point is that the questioner did not provide supporting documents. Since there was no original text in the input, the model had no choice but to piece together information that looked like a paper from the patterns it had learned. The main cause is lack of context where the required data is not in the input.

steps.title: Step 3: Check creation method
steps.body: The fact that the title, author, year, volume number, and page number match each other without discrepancy may be the result of using a probabilistically plausible combination. The more elaborate the form, the more reliable it appears, but the completeness of the form is not evidence of existence. The method of creation is also a major factor.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: The main cause in this case is the lack of context and the way it is created, with the knowledge cutoff being a secondary factor. If you divide the causes this way, the response will also be different. If there is a lack of context, provide supporting documents. If it is a problem with the creation method, you should say you do not know and check the source yourself.

screens.outro: Now that we've broken down the causes, let's see how we can actually reduce errors by changing the request.

screens.title: Commentary: Say you don't know and check with the source
screens.lead: Press the switch to alternately compare the request before responding with the request after responding.

states.label: Before responding
states.body:
Request: “Please tell me a paper on the impact of working from home on productivity.”

There is no supporting data for this request, and it does not say that if you don't know, you can say you don't know. The model can bridge plausible thesis information under pressure to answer the question. The expected response is a confident list of titles, authors, and page numbers. Whether this is true or not cannot be determined from this response alone. Moreover, because it has a plausible format, it is easy for reviewers to pass it by without checking. The question method leaves the conditions that lead to errors intact. This request method does not provide any way to verify that the result is correct.

states.label: After response
states.body:
Request: "Please answer based only on the documents attached below. First, quote the sentences related to the question directly from the original text, and then answer. Include supporting citations for each claim, and if you cannot find a citation, remove the claim. If it is not in the document, you can say you don't know."

The Claude article explains that simply telling people it's okay to say they don't know can significantly reduce disinformation. If it is a long document, citations may be drawn first, all claims checked with citations, and general knowledge outside of the provided document may be restricted. The final confirmation still rests with humans. Open the original text and link directly and compare them. Changing the request this way opens the way for the model to respond that it doesn't know, instead of making things up when it doesn't find evidence.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will organize the contents so far into one standard.

screens.title: Criteria for dealing with hallucination
screens.lead: We organize what we have seen so far into standards for how we work.

paragraphs: A model is not a database storing facts, but a tool that creates plausible sentences based on learned patterns. Different sentences in the same question are not a malfunction, but a natural result of the method of selecting tokens based on probability. Rather, the shaking part tells you where to check.

When you see an error, try dividing the cause into three parts. If it's something outside the model's range of knowledge, it's a problem with the knowledge cutoff, lack of context if you haven't provided the necessary data, or a problem with the creation method if you're deceived by your confident tone. Depending on the cause, the response will vary, including linking to a search tool, providing supporting documents, or directly checking the source.

OpenAI Help advises you to write the AI's answer as a draft, not as a final evidence, and to check important quotes and figures yourself. The degree of verification should vary depending on the task. If you distinguish between answers that can be corrected even if they are wrong and answers that cannot be wrong, you can set the time to spend on checking. This classification becomes a standard that can be used when assigning the next task.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: A confident tone is not a basis for accuracy. Let them know that it's okay to say they don't know, cite supporting information, and check the original text for important information.

glossary.def: This is a method of continuing sentences by selecting the next token based on probability. Even the same question can be worded differently.
This is a phenomenon in which a model creates plausible information that is different from the facts or does not exist.
This is the last point in time on which the model learned data. Anything after that will not be reflected unless you use the tool.
This involves checking whether the evidence provided in the answer is true by directly comparing it with the original text and the link.

misconceptions.myth: AI searches stored facts and answers.
misconceptions.fact: The model generates sentences based on the learned patterns. So even facts or sources that do not exist can be made plausible.

misconceptions.myth: If I say this confidently, it is the correct answer.
misconceptions.fact: OpenAI help explains that the model can express high confidence even in incorrect answers. Phrase and accuracy are two different things, so you need to check the basis.

misconceptions.myth: If the answers to the same question are different, the model is broken.
misconceptions.fact: It is natural that the expression varies in the way tokens are selected based on probability. However, parts that fluctuate in each response, such as the numbers, are points where you need to check the basis.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The model generates plausible sentences by picking the next token with probability rather than from a database of facts.
The roots of errors can be divided into knowledge cutoff, lack of context, and generation method.
Asking the same questions multiple times to find where you're shaky will help you know where to check.
Let them know that they can say they don't know, cite supporting evidence, and finally check directly with the original text.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What answers can and cannot be wrong in my work?

title: Probabilistic generation and the causes of hallucination

checks.q: I sent the same question three times and the conclusion was the same, but only one response had an unsourced percentage figure. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Those numbers may be unfounded, so you should check the original text.
The answer with numbers is the most detailed, so choose it.
Since the conclusion is the same, all figures can be trusted.
If the answers to the same question are different, the model is broken.
checks.explain: Numbers that vary from response to response may be a sign of lack of evidence. The starting point for confirmation is to repeat the same prompt several times to determine which parts are consistent and which are unstable.

wrong.1: Just because it's detailed doesn't mean it's accurate.
wrong.2: Even if the conclusion is the same, the detailed figures may fluctuate.
wrong.3: Since it is selected probabilistically, it is normal for the sentences to vary.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match the following examples with the closest root of hallucination
left: When asked about the results of an event held yesterday without any tools, the answer was old information.
Since no supporting documents were provided, I answered by filling in the blanks with guesses.
Answer vague questions clearly and in a plausible tone.
checks.explain: What happens after the learning point is a knowledge standard problem, and if the necessary data is not included in the input, there is a lack of context and probability is used, so a confident speaking style is not necessarily accurate.
checks.intro: Check your concepts by matching cases and causes. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: What is an appropriate way to reduce false information when asking people to answer based on a long document?
options: Ask them to answer in a more confident tone
First, have them select passages that are quoted directly from the original text and then answer them.
Try to mix in as much general knowledge as possible outside of the document.
Allows the argument to be maintained even if no citation is found.
checks.explain: If you first select supporting citations and add citations to each claim, and if you cannot find a citation and then withdraw the claim, the amount of made-up content will decrease. The last step is human verification of the original text.

wrong.0: Confident speech does not make it more accurate.
wrong.2: You can also limit the use of knowledge outside the document.
wrong.3: If no citation is found, the argument is withdrawn.

checks.intro: Remember the response methods you learned and choose the appropriate option. Results are not recorded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's unfortunate, but other options are better.
